questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: A bank is a business that accepts deposits (money people put in accounts) and makes loans (money it lends and expects to be paid back with interest). Banks keep only part of their deposits as cash and lend much of the rest. The interest borrowers pay helps the bank pay its costs, earn a profit, and pay interest to savers.
questions.question: Maya deposits $500 of her summer earnings at a bank. What does the bank usually do with much of the money while it sits in her account?

choices.text: Lends part of it to other customers, such as car buyers or businesses
Keeps her exact bills in a locked box with her name on it
Sends it to the government until she withdraws it
Invests all of it in the stock market on Maya's behalf, and she keeps any gains

questions.correct_answer: Lends part of it to other customers, such as car buyers or businesses

misconceptions.B: Thinks a bank stores each customer's own cash separately
misconceptions.C: Confuses a bank deposit with a tax payment
misconceptions.D: Confuses a bank deposit with an investment account

questions.feedback: Banks pool deposits and lend much of the money to borrowers. Maya can still withdraw her $500; the bank keeps enough cash and reserves on hand to meet withdrawals.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: A credit union offers many of the same services as a bank: checking and savings accounts, debit cards, and loans. The difference is ownership. A credit union is a not-for-profit cooperative owned by its members, who are its account holders. To join, you must meet its membership rules, such as living in an area, working for an employer, or belonging to a group.
questions.question: Which statement best describes a credit union?

choices.text: A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members
A government office that issues credit cards
A company that only sells stocks and bonds
A bank owned by outside investors who buy its stock and are not its customers

questions.correct_answer: A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members

misconceptions.B: Thinks "credit" in the name means the government provides credit
misconceptions.C: Confuses a credit union with a brokerage firm
misconceptions.D: Describes a stock-owned bank, not a credit union

questions.feedback: Credit unions are member-owned, not-for-profit cooperatives. Profits are returned to members through lower fees, lower loan rates, or higher savings rates.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: Every credit union has a "field of membership": the group of people it is allowed to serve. It might be employees of certain companies, people who live or work in a county, or members of an organization. Family members of current members can often join too. Some credit unions let almost anyone join by first joining a partner organization.
questions.question: Jordan wants to join Riverside Teachers Credit Union, but Jordan is not a teacher and has no family member who works in a school. What is the most likely obstacle?

choices.text: Jordan may not meet the credit union's membership rules
Credit unions do not offer checking accounts
Jordan must buy stock in the credit union on a stock exchange
Credit unions only accept customers who already have a credit card

questions.correct_answer: Jordan may not meet the credit union's membership rules

misconceptions.B: Thinks credit unions offer only loans
misconceptions.C: Confuses member ownership with buying publicly traded shares
misconceptions.D: Thinks a credit card is required to open an account

questions.feedback: A credit union can serve only people within its field of membership. Jordan should check its eligibility rules or look for a credit union whose field includes Jordan.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.intro: Banks come in different types. National and regional banks are large and have many branches. Community banks are smaller and local. Online banks have no branches; customers use an app, a website, ATMs, and mobile deposit. Deposits at federally insured banks are protected by the FDIC, and deposits at federally insured credit unions by the NCUA, up to legal limits.
questions.question: A city has a large national bank, a local community bank, a credit union, and an online-only bank. Which feature is TRUE of all four kinds of institutions?

choices.text: They can offer federally insured deposit accounts
They are all owned by the customers who keep accounts there
They all have branches where you can deposit cash in person
They all guarantee a profit on money you invest with them

questions.correct_answer: They can offer federally insured deposit accounts

misconceptions.B: Credit union ownership applied to every institution
misconceptions.D: Confuses insured deposits with guaranteed investment returns

questions.feedback: Federally insured banks (FDIC) and credit unions (NCUA) can all offer insured deposit accounts. Ownership, branches, and fees differ from one institution to another.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans
questions.question: Priya keeps $1,200 in cash in a shoebox. Which risk would a federally insured bank account reduce?

choices.text: The money buying less in the future because prices rise
Having to pay sales tax when she spends the money
Spending the money on things she does not need
Losing the money to a fire or theft at home

questions.correct_answer: Losing the money to a fire or theft at home

misconceptions.A: Thinks a bank account removes the effect of inflation
misconceptions.B: Confuses where money is kept with taxes on purchases
misconceptions.C: Thinks an account controls spending habits by itself

questions.feedback: Insured deposits are protected from loss at home and from bank failure up to legal limits. An account does not stop prices from rising and does not decide how she spends.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.intro: A deposit is money you put into an account. A withdrawal is money you take out. A loan is money a lender gives you that you must pay back, usually with interest.
questions.question: Aiden puts $40 into his savings account. What is this called?

choices.text: A deposit
A withdrawal
A loan
A fee

questions.correct_answer: A deposit

misconceptions.C: Thinks putting money in is borrowing
misconceptions.D: Confuses adding money with a charge

questions.feedback: Putting money into an account is a deposit. Taking money out is a withdrawal.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.intro: When you take money out of your own account, by cash at an ATM, a debit card purchase, or a check, it is a withdrawal. The money was already yours.
questions.question: Sofia takes $60 in cash out of her checking account at an ATM. What is this called?

choices.text: A withdrawal
A deposit
A loan from the ATM company
Interest

questions.correct_answer: A withdrawal

misconceptions.D: Confuses money taken out with money earned

questions.feedback: Taking your own money out of your account is a withdrawal; you do not owe it back.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.intro: A loan is borrowed money. The borrower promises to repay the amount borrowed, called the principal, plus interest, which is the price of borrowing.
questions.question: A bank gives Luis $8,000 to buy a used car, and Luis agrees to pay it back over four years with interest. What did Luis receive?

choices.text: A deposit
A gift from the bank
A withdrawal from his savings
A loan

questions.correct_answer: A loan

misconceptions.A: Thinks money received from a bank is a deposit
misconceptions.C: Confuses borrowed money with his own savings

questions.feedback: Money that must be repaid with interest is a loan. Luis owes the $8,000 principal plus interest.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.intro: Interest works in two directions. A borrower pays interest to a lender for using the lender's money. A saver earns interest from a bank, because the bank uses the saver's deposits to make loans.
questions.question: Which choice describes interest from a SAVER'S point of view?

choices.text: Money you pay the bank each month to keep your savings account open
The amount you first deposited
A tax on savings accounts
Money the bank pays you for keeping your money in an account

questions.correct_answer: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money in an account

misconceptions.A: Confuses interest with a monthly fee

questions.feedback: Savers earn interest; borrowers pay interest. The first amount deposited is the principal.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.question: Why can a bank afford to pay interest to savers?

choices.text: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers
The federal government pays the interest on every insured savings account
It charges savers a fee equal to the interest
It prints new money to pay interest

questions.correct_answer: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers

misconceptions.C: Thinks interest is cancelled by a fee
misconceptions.D: Confuses a bank with the central bank

questions.feedback: A bank earns more interest from loans than it pays on deposits. The difference helps cover costs and profit.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.intro: Many apps that hold money are not banks. They are financial technology ("fintech") companies that partner with a bank. Money may be FDIC insured only if it is actually deposited at the partner bank in the customer's name and the records are kept properly. If the fintech company itself fails, getting access to money can take time.
questions.question: A payment app advertises "bank-level" accounts. Its fine print says, "We are a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services are provided by Harbor Bank, Member FDIC." What does this mean?

choices.text: The app company is itself an FDIC-insured bank, so it is fully protected
No money in the app can ever be insured
Harbor Bank guarantees the app company's profits
Harbor Bank holds the deposits; the app company itself is not a bank

questions.correct_answer: Harbor Bank holds the deposits; the app company itself is not a bank

misconceptions.A: Takes the advertising at face value
misconceptions.B: Ignores insurance through a partner bank
misconceptions.C: Misreads what a partner bank does

questions.feedback: The fine print says the deposits are at Harbor Bank. FDIC insurance protects against Harbor Bank failing, not against the app company failing.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.intro: Deposit insurance covers money in deposit accounts at insured banks. A balance kept in a payment app may not be a bank deposit at all, depending on how the app holds it. The app's terms explain where the money is held.
questions.question: Which question is MOST useful to ask before keeping a large balance in a payment app?

choices.text: Is my balance held at an FDIC-insured bank in my name?
How many millions of people already use and trust the app?
Does the app have a nice design?
Can I send money to friends instantly?

questions.correct_answer: Is my balance held at an FDIC-insured bank in my name?

misconceptions.D: Focuses on features rather than protection

questions.feedback: Whether the balance is a deposit at an insured bank, in your name, decides whether deposit insurance can apply.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.intro: Online banks often pay higher savings rates and charge fewer fees because they have no branches to run. The trade-off is access: depositing cash can be hard or impossible, and help is by phone or chat. The best choice depends on how you use your money.
questions.question: An online bank pays 4.0% on savings and charges no monthly fee, but it has no branches. A local bank pays 0.5% and has a branch near Ana's job. Ana is paid in cash tips each night. Which drawback of the online bank matters MOST for Ana?

choices.text: Depositing cash may be difficult without a branch
The online bank's savings rate is too high
Online banks are not allowed to give customers debit cards
Online banks are never insured

questions.correct_answer: Depositing cash may be difficult without a branch

misconceptions.B: Thinks a higher savings rate is a drawback
misconceptions.C: Assumes online banks lack debit cards
misconceptions.D: Assumes no online bank is insured

questions.feedback: Ana deposits cash every night, so a way to deposit cash matters more to her than a higher rate. She might use both kinds of bank.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.question: A bank's website shows the FDIC logo. What does this tell a customer?

choices.text: The bank's stock price is guaranteed
Every product the bank sells is insured, including investments
The bank charges no fees
Its deposits are insured up to the legal limit

questions.correct_answer: Its deposits are insured up to the legal limit

misconceptions.A: Thinks FDIC insures a bank's stock

questions.feedback: The FDIC sign means deposits are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Investments sold at a bank are not deposits and are not FDIC insured.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.section_skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks
questions.question: Which situation shows the main risk of keeping money with a non-bank app?

choices.text: The partner bank pays interest into each customer's account every month
The app sends a monthly statement
The customer uses the app's debit card at a store
The app company fails and customers wait months to reach their money

questions.correct_answer: The app company fails and customers wait months to reach their money

misconceptions.A: Describes an advantage, not a risk

questions.feedback: When a fintech company fails, its records of who owns what must be sorted out before customers can get their money, even if a partner bank is insured.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.intro: Fees add up. A monthly fee costs 12 times that amount in a year. Many banks waive a monthly fee if you meet a condition, such as a minimum balance or a direct deposit. If you will not meet the condition, plan to pay the fee.
questions.question: Two banks are similar except: Bank A charges a $12 monthly fee unless the balance stays above $1,500; Bank B charges no monthly fee. Kai usually keeps about $400 in checking. How much more would Bank A cost Kai per year?

misconceptions.B: Uses one month instead of a year

questions.feedback: Kai's $400 balance is below $1,500, so the fee applies every month: $12 × 12 = $144.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.intro: When comparing institutions, start with how you will use the account: fees, ATM access, branch or app access, minimum balances, and the savings rate. A feature that matters to one person may not matter to another.
questions.question: Which comparison is MOST important for a student who will make frequent ATM withdrawals?

choices.text: How many fee-free ATMs are near home and school
Whether the bank sponsors a local sports team or event
The color of the debit card
The bank's auto loan rate

questions.correct_answer: How many fee-free ATMs are near home and school

misconceptions.D: Compares a product the student will not use now

questions.feedback: Frequent ATM users can pay fees each time they use an out-of-network ATM, so fee-free ATM access is the key comparison.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.intro: To compare savings rates, find the interest each account pays. For one year, interest ≈ balance × rate (with the rate written as a decimal). Then subtract.
questions.question: A credit union and a bank both offer free checking. The credit union pays 2.5% on savings; the bank pays 0.1%. On a $2,000 savings balance for one year (simple interest), how much more would the credit union pay?

misconceptions.D: Uses only the credit union's interest

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.question: Which document lists every fee an account can charge, such as overdraft, wire, and paper statement fees?

choices.text: The account's fee schedule
The bank's home page advertisement
A monthly statement from last year
The debit card itself

questions.correct_answer: The account's fee schedule

misconceptions.C: Thinks a statement lists every possible fee
misconceptions.D: Thinks fees are printed on the card

questions.feedback: Banks give a fee schedule (often part of the account agreement). Ads show the highlights; the fee schedule shows every charge.

questions.set_title: Banks, credit unions, and what they do
questions.question: Leo picks a bank only because it gave him a $200 bonus for opening an account. Six months later he notices $15 monthly fees. What step did he skip?

choices.text: Asking the bank for a larger bonus before opening
Opening the account online
Getting a credit card from the same bank first
Reading the fee conditions before choosing

questions.correct_answer: Reading the fee conditions before choosing

misconceptions.A: Treats the bonus as the main decision
misconceptions.B: Thinks the method of opening caused the fees
misconceptions.C: Thinks a credit card prevents account fees

questions.feedback: Six months of $15 fees is $90, and the fees continue every month. Bonuses often require conditions; the fee rules decide the long-run cost.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: A checking account is a bank or credit union account for everyday money: receiving pay, paying bills, buying things with a debit card, and writing checks. Checking accounts usually pay little or no interest. Money you are setting aside for later usually goes in a savings account.
questions.question: Tia's paycheck is deposited into her checking account. Which use is a checking account designed for?

choices.text: Earning high interest on long-term savings
Buying shares of stock
Borrowing money for a car
Paying rent, bills, and everyday purchases

questions.correct_answer: Paying rent, bills, and everyday purchases

misconceptions.B: Confuses checking with a brokerage account
misconceptions.C: Confuses an account with a loan

questions.feedback: Checking accounts are transaction accounts for everyday spending and bills. Long-term savings and investments belong in other accounts.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: A debit card is linked to your checking account. When you pay with it, the money comes out of your account, usually within a day or two. A credit card is different: the card company lends you the money, and you pay it back later.
questions.question: Noah buys groceries for $46.30 with his debit card. Where does the money come from?

choices.text: Directly from Noah's checking account
From a loan that Noah repays next month
From the store's bank account
From Noah's savings account automatically, every time

questions.correct_answer: Directly from Noah's checking account

misconceptions.B: Confuses a debit card with a credit card
misconceptions.D: Thinks debit cards draw from savings

questions.feedback: A debit card spends money already in the linked checking account. It is not a loan.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: Your balance is the money in your account. Each withdrawal, debit card purchase, or bill payment is subtracted; each deposit is added. Keeping a running balance helps you avoid spending money you do not have.
questions.question: Ella's checking balance is $312.40. She pays a $95.25 phone bill and makes a $40.00 ATM withdrawal. What is her new balance?

misconceptions.D: Adds the payments instead of subtracting

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: Some merchants, such as gas stations, hotels, and car rentals, place a temporary "hold" on a debit card before they know the final amount. The hold lowers your AVAILABLE balance (what you can spend now) until the final charge posts and the extra is released, often within a few days.
questions.question: At a gas pump, Sam's debit card is approved, and the bank places a $100 hold, even though Sam pumps only $38 of gas. What is the effect until the hold is released?

choices.text: Sam is charged $100 permanently
Sam's account balance goes up by $62
Nothing changes, because holds only apply to credit cards
Sam's available balance is $100 lower for a short time

questions.correct_answer: Sam's available balance is $100 lower for a short time

misconceptions.A: Thinks a hold is the final charge
misconceptions.C: Thinks holds only apply to credit cards

questions.feedback: The hold temporarily reduces the available balance by $100. When the $38 charge posts, the extra $62 is released.

questions.section_skill: Use a checking account and debit card and track the available balance
questions.intro: Federal law limits what you owe when a card is used without permission. For credit cards, the most you can owe for unauthorized charges is $50. For debit cards, the limit depends on how quickly you report the loss: $50, $500, or more if you wait over 60 days after your statement. Debit card fraud also removes your own money until the bank investigates.
questions.question: A thief steals Ava's wallet and uses both her debit card and her credit card. Which card generally gives her stronger legal protection against the thief's charges?

choices.text: The credit card
The debit card, because it spends her own money
The debit card, because banks must refund theft the same day
Both cards always have identical protection

questions.correct_answer: The credit card

misconceptions.B: Assumes spending your own money gives more protection

questions.feedback: Federal law caps credit card liability for unauthorized charges at $50. Debit card liability depends on how quickly you report the loss: up to $50, up to $500, or more after 60 days. Meanwhile, a thief has spent your own money.

questions.intro: "Debit" means taking money out of your account. A debit card takes money from your checking account. "Credit" means borrowing: a credit card company pays the store, and you owe the card company.
questions.question: Which card spends money that is ALREADY in your bank account?

choices.text: A debit card
A credit card
A store gift card from a friend
A library card

questions.correct_answer: A debit card

misconceptions.B: Thinks a credit card spends your own money
misconceptions.C: Confuses a prepaid gift card with a bank account card

questions.feedback: A debit card draws on money already in your checking account.

questions.intro: With a credit card, the card company pays the merchant for you. The amount is added to your card balance, which is a debt you must pay back. If you do not pay the full balance by the due date, you may owe interest.
questions.question: Owen pays for a $25 meal with a credit card. Who pays the restaurant first?

choices.text: Owen's checking account, immediately
The restaurant pays itself
Nobody pays the restaurant until Owen gets his monthly bill
The credit card company, and Owen owes it $25

questions.correct_answer: The credit card company, and Owen owes it $25

misconceptions.C: Thinks the store waits to be paid

questions.feedback: The card company pays the restaurant; Owen now owes the card company $25.

questions.intro: A debit card can only spend the money in your account. If a purchase is larger than your balance, the bank may decline it. If you opted in to overdraft coverage, the bank may pay it and charge an overdraft fee.
questions.question: What happens if you try to spend more with a debit card than your account holds?

choices.text: The extra amount becomes a free gift
The store lowers the price to your balance
Your credit card is charged automatically, every time
It is declined, or covered for an overdraft fee

questions.correct_answer: It is declined, or covered for an overdraft fee

misconceptions.A: Thinks the bank absorbs the shortfall for free
misconceptions.B: Thinks the store adjusts the price
misconceptions.C: Thinks a credit card always backs a debit card

questions.feedback: Spending past your balance leads to a declined purchase or an overdraft with a fee.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE?

choices.text: Using a credit card creates a debt; using a debit card does not
Using a debit card creates a debt; using a credit card does not
Both cards always create a debt
Neither card is ever connected to money you owe

questions.correct_answer: Using a credit card creates a debt; using a debit card does not
questions.feedback: Credit cards are borrowing. Debit cards spend your own money.

questions.intro: If you do not opt in to overdraft coverage, a bank generally cannot charge you an overdraft fee for an ATM withdrawal or a one-time debit card purchase; instead the purchase is declined. A credit card lets you borrow up to a credit limit, which is not your money.
questions.question: Mia wants a card that will stop her from spending more than she has. Which card fits that goal better?

choices.text: A credit card with a high limit
A credit card that she uses only for large purchases
Any card, because cards cannot be overspent
A debit card with overdraft coverage turned off

questions.correct_answer: A debit card with overdraft coverage turned off

misconceptions.A: Thinks a credit limit is her own money
misconceptions.B: Thinks purchase size changes how credit works

questions.feedback: Without overdraft coverage, one-time debit card purchases above the balance are generally declined, so Mia cannot spend money she does not have.

questions.intro: An ATM network is a group of machines your bank lets you use without a fee. At an "out-of-network" ATM you can be charged twice: once by your own bank and once by the ATM's owner (a "surcharge").
questions.question: Rosa uses an out-of-network ATM. Her bank charges $2.50 and the ATM owner charges $3.00. She withdraws $40. How much leaves her account in total?

misconceptions.C: Includes only the ATM owner's fee

questions.intro: Small fees repeated often add up. Multiply the fee per use by the number of uses in a year.
questions.question: Rosa makes that same kind of out-of-network withdrawal twice a week. About how much does she pay in ATM fees in a year (52 weeks)?

misconceptions.A: Gives the fees for one withdrawal
misconceptions.D: Includes the $40 cash withdrawn each time

questions.feedback: Fees per withdrawal: $2.50 + $3.00 = $5.50. Withdrawals per year: 2 × 52 = 104. Fees: $5.50 × 104 = $572.

questions.question: Which choice would cut Rosa's ATM fees the MOST?

choices.text: Use in-network ATMs or get cash back at stores
Withdraw $20 each time instead of $40
Use a different out-of-network ATM each time she needs cash
Check her balance at the ATM before each withdrawal

questions.correct_answer: Use in-network ATMs or get cash back at stores

misconceptions.B: Smaller withdrawals mean more fees, not fewer
misconceptions.C: Thinks a different machine avoids fees

questions.feedback: In-network ATMs and cash back at stores usually have no fees. Smaller, more frequent withdrawals raise the total fees.

questions.intro: Some accounts refund ATM fees up to a monthly limit. The refund lowers what you pay, but only up to that limit.
questions.question: A bank refunds up to $10 of other banks' ATM fees each month. Rosa pays $22 in out-of-network fees this month. How much does she pay after the refund?

misconceptions.A: Gives the refund instead of what she pays

questions.question: Which statement about an ATM "balance inquiry" at an out-of-network machine is MOST accurate?

choices.text: It is always free, because no money leaves the account
It moves money to savings
It counts as a deposit
It can carry a fee even though no money is withdrawn

questions.correct_answer: It can carry a fee even though no money is withdrawn

misconceptions.A: Assumes balance checks are free at any ATM
misconceptions.B: Confuses an inquiry with a transfer
misconceptions.C: Confuses an inquiry with a deposit

questions.feedback: Out-of-network ATMs may charge for balance checks. Checking the balance in your bank's app is usually free.

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.intro: A transaction is "pending" when the bank knows about it but has not finished processing it ("posting" it). Your available balance is the money you can spend now: roughly your posted balance minus pending charges and holds. Spending based on the larger number can cause overdrafts.
questions.question: Kim's app shows: current balance $250; pending transactions −$80. What is her available balance?

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.intro: Bank apps show what the bank knows. A check you wrote that the payee has not cashed yet does not appear at all. Your own record of payments, called a register, catches those.
questions.question: Which balance should Kim use to decide whether she can afford a $150 purchase today?

choices.text: Her available balance minus uncleared checks
The highest balance she had this month
Her balance from last month's statement
Her current balance, without counting pending items

questions.correct_answer: Her available balance minus uncleared checks
questions.feedback: Her real spending power is the available balance minus payments the bank has not seen yet.

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.intro: When you deposit a check, the bank may "hold" part of the money until the check clears. Federal rules set the maximum hold times, and the bank must tell you when the money will be available.
questions.question: Ben deposits a $600 check on Monday. The bank says $225 is available Tuesday and the rest Thursday. How much can Ben safely spend from this deposit on Tuesday?

misconceptions.D: Assumes the whole deposit is available at once
misconceptions.C: Gives the amount held until Thursday
misconceptions.A: Thinks none of a check is available early

questions.feedback: Only $225 is available Tuesday; the remaining $375 becomes available Thursday.

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.question: If a deposited check "bounces" (is returned unpaid) after you spent the money, what usually happens?

choices.text: The bank takes the amount back from your account, possibly with a fee
The bank keeps the money in your account because it was already available
The person who wrote the check pays your fee
Nothing, because the deposit was already posted

questions.correct_answer: The bank takes the amount back from your account, possibly with a fee

misconceptions.C: Assumes fees are always passed on
misconceptions.D: Thinks a posted deposit cannot be reversed

questions.feedback: A returned check is reversed out of your account. If you already spent the money, your balance can go negative, and fees may apply. This is how fake-check scams harm victims.

questions.section_skill: Pending transactions, available balance, and posting
questions.question: Which habit best prevents spending based on the wrong balance?

choices.text: Checking the balance once a month
Using only the current balance on the bank app
Keeping your PIN on the card
Recording each purchase as you make it

questions.correct_answer: Recording each purchase as you make it

misconceptions.B: Ignores pending items and uncleared checks

questions.feedback: Recording each transaction as it happens keeps your own balance current, including items the bank has not seen yet.

questions.section_skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one
questions.intro: Banks and credit unions usually require an adult (18 or older) to open an account alone, because a minor generally cannot be held to a contract. Many offer teen or student checking accounts that a minor opens jointly with a parent or guardian. The adult co-owner can see the account and shares responsibility for it.
questions.question: Jordan is 17 and wants a first checking account. Which plan matches how most banks handle an applicant under 18?

choices.text: Open a joint teen account with a parent or guardian
Open an individual account online using only a student ID card
Wait until age 21, the legal minimum age for any bank account
Deposit paychecks into a friend's account until Jordan turns 18

questions.correct_answer: Open a joint teen account with a parent or guardian

misconceptions.B: Thinks a school ID meets the identity requirements
misconceptions.C: Invents a minimum age for every account
misconceptions.D: Thinks sharing someone else's account is safe or allowed

questions.feedback: Most institutions let a minor open a checking account only as a joint or teen account with an adult co-owner.

questions.section_skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one
questions.intro: Federal rules require banks to verify who opens an account. Before opening one, a bank collects at least your name, date of birth, address, and an identification number: a Social Security number for U.S. citizens, or another number, such as an ITIN or passport number, for others. Most banks also ask for a government-issued photo ID.
questions.question: Which information will a bank most likely require to open a checking account?

choices.text: Your report card, a teacher's reference, and your school's address
Your credit card number and its PIN, to link the two accounts
Only a signature, because banks do not verify who customers are
Name, birth date, address, and an ID number such as an SSN

questions.correct_answer: Name, birth date, address, and an ID number such as an SSN

misconceptions.B: Thinks sharing a PIN is part of opening an account

questions.feedback: The Customer Identification Program rule requires name, date of birth, address, and an ID number; banks usually also check a photo ID.

questions.section_skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one
questions.intro: Many checking accounts charge a monthly maintenance fee that is waived if you meet a condition: a minimum balance, a minimum direct deposit, or being a student. Compare accounts by the fees YOU would actually pay, based on how you will use the account.
questions.question:
Tess will receive about $800 a month by direct deposit and usually keeps about $300 in checking.
Account X: $10 monthly fee, waived with a direct deposit of $500 or more each month.
Account Y: $5 monthly fee, waived if the balance stays at $1,000 or more.
What would each account cost Tess in monthly fees over a year?

choices.text: Account X: $120; Account Y: $60
Account X: $0; Account Y: $0
Account X: $120; Account Y: $0
Account X: $0; Account Y: $60

questions.correct_answer: Account X: $0; Account Y: $60

misconceptions.A: Ignores Account X's direct deposit waiver
misconceptions.B: Assumes Tess meets Account Y's $1,000 balance rule

questions.feedback: Tess's $800 direct deposit meets Account X's $500 condition, so X costs $0. Her $300 balance is below Y's $1,000, so Y costs $5 × 12 = $60.

questions.section_skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one
questions.intro: Direct deposit sends pay electronically into your account. Your employer needs two numbers: the routing number, a 9-digit number that identifies your bank, and your account number, which identifies your account at that bank. Both appear on checks and in the bank's app. Never share a PIN or password to set up a deposit.
questions.question: Tess wants her paycheck deposited directly into her new account. What does her employer need from her?

choices.text: Her bank's routing number and her account number
Her debit card number and its PIN
Her online banking username and password
Only the name of her bank and the branch's street address

questions.correct_answer: Her bank's routing number and her account number

misconceptions.B: Confuses a debit card with the account itself; unsafe
misconceptions.C: Thinks an employer needs login credentials; unsafe
misconceptions.D: Thinks a bank name identifies a specific account

questions.feedback: Routing number plus account number tells the payroll system exactly where to send the money. PINs and passwords are never needed.

questions.section_skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one
questions.question: Ahmed's new account requires a $25 opening deposit and has a $6 monthly fee that is waived only when the balance stays at $300 or more. Ahmed's balance stays around $150. Assuming no other fees, how much will the account charge him in fees over 6 months?

misconceptions.D: Adds the opening deposit as if it were a fee

questions.feedback: The fee applies every month because $150 is below $300: $6 × 6 = $36. The $25 opening deposit is Ahmed's own money in the account, not a fee.

questions.intro: A fee is a charge the bank takes from your account. A "monthly maintenance fee" (also called a service fee) is charged every month just for having the account, unless you meet a waiver condition.
questions.question: A checking account has a "$12 monthly maintenance fee." What does this mean?

choices.text: The bank takes $12 each month unless a waiver applies
The bank pays you $12 each month for keeping the account
You must deposit $12 every month to keep the account open
You pay $12 one time, when you first open the account

questions.correct_answer: The bank takes $12 each month unless a waiver applies

misconceptions.C: Confuses a fee with a deposit requirement
misconceptions.D: Thinks a monthly fee is charged once

questions.feedback: A monthly maintenance fee is taken from your account each month unless you qualify for a waiver.

questions.intro: A waiver condition is a rule that, if you meet it, cancels a fee. A "minimum daily balance" rule means your balance must stay at or above the amount every day of the statement period.
questions.question: An account waives its $8 monthly fee "with a minimum daily balance of $500." In March, Lena's balance stays above $600 every day. What fee does she pay for March?

misconceptions.D: Confuses the balance requirement with a fee

questions.feedback: Lena's balance never dropped below $500, so the fee is waived: $0.

questions.intro: With a minimum daily balance rule, one day below the minimum is enough to lose the waiver for that month, even if the balance is high on other days.
questions.question: Using the same account, Lena's balance drops to $450 for one day in April, then goes back above $600. What fee does she pay for April?

misconceptions.A: Uses the average or ending balance instead of the daily minimum

questions.feedback: One day at $450 is below $500, so the $8 fee applies for April.

questions.question: Which statement about a minimum opening deposit is TRUE?

choices.text: It is a fee the bank keeps to open the account
It is a loan the bank gives you to start the account
It must be paid again every month you keep the account
It is your own money, deposited into your new account

questions.correct_answer: It is your own money, deposited into your new account

misconceptions.A: Confuses a deposit with a fee
misconceptions.B: Confuses a deposit with a loan
misconceptions.C: Confuses an opening deposit with a monthly fee

questions.feedback: An opening deposit is the first money you put into the account. It stays yours.

questions.question: Two accounts are identical except for fees. Which would cost a student nothing?

choices.text: One with a $3 fee, because the fee is small
One with a $15 fee waived at a $5,000 balance, for a student with $200
One with a fee charged only every other month, at $6
One whose fee is waived for students, if the student qualifies

questions.correct_answer: One whose fee is waived for students, if the student qualifies

misconceptions.A: Thinks a small fee is the same as no fee
misconceptions.B: Ignores whether the student can meet the waiver
misconceptions.C: Overlooks that $6 every other month still adds up

questions.feedback: Only an account whose fee the student can actually avoid costs nothing.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.intro: When you open an account, the bank gives you disclosures: documents that list the account's interest rate, fees, and rules. Federal law (the Truth in Savings Act) requires banks to disclose this information. Small optional fees, like paper statement fees, are easy to miss.
questions.question: A disclosure says: "Paper statement fee: $2 per month. Free with e-statements." Rafael wants paper statements. Over two years, how much will this choice cost?
questions.feedback: $2 per month × 24 months = $48.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.intro: A fee schedule is a list of every fee the account can charge: monthly fees, overdraft and returned item fees, wire transfer fees, stop payment fees, out-of-network ATM fees, and fees for extras like paper statements or cashier's checks.
questions.question: Which item would you expect to find in an account's fee schedule?

choices.text: The charge for an incoming or outgoing wire transfer
The bank's current interest rate on 30-year home mortgages
The FDIC insurance limit for your account
The interest rate on your credit card

questions.correct_answer: The charge for an incoming or outgoing wire transfer

misconceptions.B: Confuses a fee schedule with a loan rate sheet
misconceptions.D: Confuses a deposit fee schedule with a card agreement

questions.feedback: Wire transfer fees are account fees listed in a fee schedule.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.question: An account advertises "No monthly fee!" Its fee schedule lists a $35 overdraft fee, a $3 out-of-network ATM fee, and a $30 wire fee. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: The account can still be costly, depending on how it is used
The account has no fees of any kind
The account will cost exactly $68 every month, since all three fees apply
Every one of those fees is illegal for a free account

questions.correct_answer: The account can still be costly, depending on how it is used

misconceptions.B: Treats the ad as the whole story
misconceptions.C: Adds possible fees as if all are charged monthly
misconceptions.D: Thinks a free account cannot have any fees

questions.feedback: "No monthly fee" covers only the maintenance fee. Other fees apply when you use certain services or overdraw.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.intro: Banks can change account terms. They must tell existing customers in advance about changes that could hurt them, such as a higher fee. That notice gives you time to compare and decide.
questions.question: A bank sends a notice that a fee will change in 30 days. What is a reasonable response?

choices.text: Ignore it, because fees cannot change after an account is opened
Close the account the same day without checking alternatives
Pay the new fee now to lock in the old rate
Compare the new terms with other accounts

questions.correct_answer: Compare the new terms with other accounts

misconceptions.A: Thinks account terms are fixed forever
misconceptions.C: Invents a way to lock in fees

questions.feedback: Advance notice lets you compare and, if needed, move your money before the change takes effect.

questions.section_skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules
questions.question: Which question is MOST useful when comparing two accounts' disclosures?

choices.text: Which bank has the larger headquarters building?
Which disclosure document is longer?
Which bank's advertising do I see most often on social media?
Which fees will I realistically pay, given how I bank?

questions.correct_answer: Which fees will I realistically pay, given how I bank?

misconceptions.A: Uses size as a measure of cost
misconceptions.B: Uses document length as a measure of cost
misconceptions.C: Uses advertising as a measure of cost

questions.feedback: Your real cost depends on your habits: balance, deposits, ATM use, and overdraft risk.

questions.intro: Before opening an account, many banks check a consumer report from a checking account screening company, such as ChexSystems or Early Warning Services. These reports list problems with past accounts, such as unpaid overdrafts, accounts closed by a bank, or suspected fraud. Negative information can stay on these reports for years.
questions.question: Devon's application for a checking account is denied because of a report from a checking account screening company. What kind of history does such a report usually show?

choices.text: Unpaid overdrafts or fraud at past banks
Grades and attendance from high school
Devon's medical history and doctor visits
Every purchase Devon has made with cash

questions.correct_answer: Unpaid overdrafts or fraud at past banks
questions.feedback: Screening reports focus on past deposit-account problems, such as unpaid negative balances or fraud.

questions.intro: Checking account screening companies are consumer reporting agencies. Under federal law you can get a free copy of your report every 12 months and dispute information you believe is wrong; the company must investigate.
questions.question: Devon thinks the report has a mistake. What can he do?

choices.text: Nothing, because screening reports cannot be corrected
Pay the screening company to delete it
Open new accounts under a friend's name instead of his own
Request a free copy of the report and dispute the error

questions.correct_answer: Request a free copy of the report and dispute the error
questions.feedback: Like credit reports, screening reports can be requested for free each year and disputed when wrong.

questions.question: Devon's report is accurate: he left a $90 negative balance at an old bank. Which step would most likely help him open an account in the future?

choices.text: Pay off the $90 and ask the old bank to update the report
Wait one week, because reports clear automatically
Open many applications at once to find one bank that says yes
Avoid banks and keep all of his money in cash

questions.correct_answer: Pay off the $90 and ask the old bank to update the report

misconceptions.D: Gives up the protection of an insured account

questions.feedback: Paying what is owed and having the record updated to "paid" improves his chances. Keeping cash at home adds theft and loss risks.

questions.intro: Some banks and credit unions offer second-chance accounts to people who were denied regular accounts. They may have a monthly fee, no overdraft feature, or lower limits. After a period of good use, some can be changed to a regular account.
questions.question: What is a "second-chance" checking account?

choices.text: A second account that the bank opens automatically for every customer
A loan that pays off your old bank's balance
A savings account that pays double interest
An account for people with past account problems, often with limits

questions.correct_answer: An account for people with past account problems, often with limits

misconceptions.B: Confuses an account with a loan

questions.feedback: Second-chance accounts help people rebuild banking history, often with limits or fees.

questions.question: Why might a second-chance account be better for Devon than using check-cashing stores for every paycheck?

choices.text: Check-cashing fees on every paycheck can cost far more over a year
Check-cashing stores are always free
Second-chance accounts pay much higher interest than savings accounts
A bank account means Devon can never overdraw again

questions.correct_answer: Check-cashing fees on every paycheck can cost far more over a year

misconceptions.B: Assumes check cashing has no fees
misconceptions.D: Thinks an account prevents all overdrafts

questions.feedback: For example, 2% of a $900 paycheck every two weeks is $18 per check, about $468 a year, which is usually much more than an account's fees.

questions.section_skill: Track a running balance and read a bank statement
questions.intro: An account register (or a budgeting app) records every transaction and keeps a running balance. Add each deposit (money in). Subtract each withdrawal, payment, or purchase (money out). Recording each item as it happens shows what you truly have.
questions.question: Nina starts with $215.60 in checking. She deposits $84.25, buys shoes for $59.99, and pays a $42.00 bill. What is her balance?

misconceptions.D: Adds the purchases instead of subtracting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deposit instead of adding

questions.section_skill: Track a running balance and read a bank statement
questions.intro: A bank statement summarizes one period, usually a month: the balance at the start, every deposit and withdrawal, any fees or interest, and the balance at the end. Ending balance = beginning balance + deposits − withdrawals.
questions.question: A bank statement shows: beginning balance $640.00; total deposits $1,120.00; total withdrawals $1,395.50. What is the ending balance?

misconceptions.D: Adds the withdrawals instead of subtracting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts withdrawals from deposits but leaves out the beginning balance
misconceptions.C: Adds the beginning balance to withdrawals and subtracts deposits

questions.section_skill: Track a running balance and read a bank statement
questions.intro: The statement equation (beginning + deposits − withdrawals = ending) can be used to find any missing amount. Substitute what you know and solve for the unknown.
questions.question: A statement shows a beginning balance of $410.00, withdrawals of $760.00, and an ending balance of $300.00. What were the total deposits?

misconceptions.B: Subtracts instead of solving for the missing amount

questions.section_skill: Track a running balance and read a bank statement
questions.intro: If more money leaves an account than it holds, the balance becomes negative: the account is "overdrawn." A negative balance is money owed to the bank, often with a fee added. It must be repaid by depositing money.
questions.question: Carlos's balance is $42.10. A $55.00 automatic payment goes through anyway. What does his account show afterward?

misconceptions.C: Ignores the sign; thinks the account still has money
misconceptions.B: Thinks a balance cannot go below zero

questions.feedback: $42.10 − $55.00 = −$12.90. Carlos owes the bank $12.90, plus any overdraft fee.

questions.section_skill: Track a running balance and read a bank statement
questions.intro: A check you write is paid only when the person you paid deposits or cashes it, which can take days or weeks. Until then, the money is still in your account, but it is already promised.
questions.question: Ivy wrote a $75 check to her landlord on May 30. Her May 31 bank statement does not show it. Why?

choices.text: The bank forgot to charge the check, so Ivy gets to keep the $75
Checks never appear on bank statements
The check was paid from Ivy's savings account automatically
The landlord had not yet deposited the check when the statement closed

questions.correct_answer: The landlord had not yet deposited the check when the statement closed

misconceptions.A: Thinks a missing item means the payment is cancelled

questions.feedback: An "outstanding" check has been written but not yet cashed. It will appear later, so Ivy's register must still subtract it.

questions.intro: Money coming into an account (deposits, direct deposits, transfers in, interest) is a credit and increases the balance. Money going out (purchases, withdrawals, bill payments, fees) is a debit and decreases it.
questions.question: Which transaction INCREASES a checking account balance?

choices.text: A paycheck deposited by direct deposit
A debit card purchase at a store
An ATM cash withdrawal
An automatic payment for this month's phone bill

questions.correct_answer: A paycheck deposited by direct deposit
questions.feedback: A deposit is money in; the other three are money out.

questions.intro: On a bank statement, "debit" means money taken out of the account, and "credit" means money added. Fees are debits; interest earned and refunds are credits.
questions.question: On a bank statement, which item is a debit?

choices.text: A $3.00 ATM fee
$0.42 of interest earned
A $200 transfer in from savings
A $50 refund from a store

questions.correct_answer: A $3.00 ATM fee

misconceptions.C: Thinks a transfer in is money out
misconceptions.D: Thinks a refund is money out

questions.feedback: The fee is taken from the account, so it is a debit.

questions.intro: Each purchase with a debit card lowers your balance by the purchase amount.
questions.question: Zoe's balance is $120. She buys a $30 jacket. What happens to her balance?

choices.text: It goes up to $150
It stays at $120 until the end of the month
It goes down to $30
It goes down to $90

questions.correct_answer: It goes down to $90

misconceptions.B: Thinks purchases wait until month end
misconceptions.C: Confuses the price with the new balance

questions.question: Why should you record a purchase in your register right away?

choices.text: Because the bank charges a fee each month if you do not record it
Because unrecorded purchases are free
Because the store needs a copy of your register
So your balance shows what you really have left to spend

questions.correct_answer: So your balance shows what you really have left to spend

misconceptions.B: Thinks unrecorded items are not charged

questions.feedback: Recording each item immediately keeps your running balance accurate.

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY items that lower a balance?

choices.text: A check you wrote, a bill payment, and a monthly fee
A deposit, a check you wrote, and a refund
Interest earned, a monthly fee, and a transfer in from savings
A paycheck, a gift deposited, and interest

questions.correct_answer: A check you wrote, a bill payment, and a monthly fee

misconceptions.D: Lists only items that add money

questions.feedback: Checks you write, bill payments, and fees are all money out.

questions.intro: Reconciling means checking that your records match the bank's. Start with the statement's ending balance, add deposits the bank has not recorded yet ("deposits in transit"), and subtract checks and payments that have not cleared ("outstanding"). The result should equal your register balance.
questions.question: Sam's statement ending balance is $520. He has a $150 deposit the bank had not received yet and two outstanding checks of $60 and $45. What is his adjusted (true) balance?

misconceptions.B: Uses the statement balance without adjusting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deposit and the checks

questions.intro: When the adjusted statement balance and the register do not match, look for items on the statement that are missing from the register, such as fees, interest, or automatic payments, and for math mistakes in the register.
questions.question: After adjusting, Sam's statement shows $565, but his register shows $575. Which is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: A $10 charge on the statement was never recorded in his register
The bank always makes small $10 errors in its own favor
Sam's deposit in transit was $10 smaller than he thought
Interest earned is never shown on statements

questions.correct_answer: A $10 charge on the statement was never recorded in his register

misconceptions.C: Would make the adjusted balance lower, not his register higher

questions.feedback: A $10 fee or charge that Sam did not record would make his register $10 too high.

questions.question: Sam finds a $4 monthly "service fee" on his statement that he did not record. What should he do in his register?

choices.text: Add $4 to his register balance
Ignore it, since the bank already recorded it
Subtract $8, once for the bank and once for him
Subtract $4 from his register balance

questions.correct_answer: Subtract $4 from his register balance

misconceptions.B: Thinks only one record needs updating

questions.feedback: A fee is money out, so Sam subtracts $4 to keep his register correct.

questions.question: Which reason BEST explains why reconciling monthly matters?

choices.text: It raises the interest rate on the account
It is legally required for every account holder
It removes any fees the bank charged that month
It catches errors and unauthorized charges early

questions.correct_answer: It catches errors and unauthorized charges early
questions.feedback: Spotting problems early matters because reporting deadlines apply to unauthorized transfers and errors.

questions.question: Amy's statement ending balance is $310. Outstanding checks: $25 and $40. No deposits in transit. Her register shows $245. Do her records agree?

choices.text: No: her register should show $310
No: her register should show $375
Yes, because the two numbers are close

questions.feedback: $310 − $65 = $245, which matches her register.

questions.intro: An unauthorized transaction is one you did not make or allow. Federal rules (Regulation E) limit your liability for unauthorized electronic transfers, but the protection depends on how fast you report. Contact your bank as soon as you notice one.
questions.question: Lucas sees a $129 charge from an online store he has never used. What should he do FIRST?

choices.text: Wait until next month to see if it happens again
Email the online store his full account number to ask about the charge
Ignore it, because small banks cannot reverse charges
Contact his bank right away to report the unauthorized charge

questions.correct_answer: Contact his bank right away to report the unauthorized charge

misconceptions.B: Shares sensitive data with an unknown party

questions.feedback: Reporting quickly keeps his liability limits as low as possible.

questions.intro: For unauthorized electronic transfers that appear on a statement, you generally have 60 days after the statement is sent to report them. After that, you may be liable for later transfers the bank could have stopped.
questions.question: Under Regulation E, an unauthorized debit card charge that did NOT involve a lost or stolen card appears on Mia's statement. Within how many days of the statement must she report it to keep full protection?

choices.text: 60 days
2 days
7 days
1 year

questions.correct_answer: 60 days

misconceptions.D: Thinks there is no practical deadline

questions.feedback: Report within 60 days of the statement date. If a card is lost or stolen, report within 2 business days of learning of it for the lowest limit ($50).

questions.question: A store charged Ana twice for one $45 purchase. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Duplicate charges are legal if the store says so
She must accept it because she used her card
This is an error she can dispute with the bank or the store
She can only fix it by closing her account

questions.correct_answer: This is an error she can dispute with the bank or the store

misconceptions.B: Thinks using the card waives rights
misconceptions.D: Thinks closing the account is the only fix

questions.feedback: A duplicate charge is an error. She can ask the store for a refund and dispute it with her bank.

questions.question: Which habit catches unauthorized charges the fastest?

choices.text: Reading paper statements once a year
Checking only the ending balance on each statement
Transaction alerts and frequent app checks
Using the card less often

questions.correct_answer: Transaction alerts and frequent app checks
questions.feedback: Alerts and frequent checks spot problems within days.

questions.intro: For a lost or stolen debit card, if you report within 2 business days of learning of the loss, your liability for unauthorized transfers is capped at $50. After 2 business days, the cap rises to $500. Many banks voluntarily offer $0 liability, but the law sets these limits.
questions.question: Ben lost his debit card on Monday, noticed it Tuesday, and reported it Tuesday. A thief spent $300 before he reported it. What is the most Ben can be held responsible for under federal rules?

choices.text: $0, in every case

misconceptions.A: Thinks he owes everything the thief spent
misconceptions.B: Uses the limit for late reports
misconceptions.C: Assumes there is never any liability

questions.feedback: He reported within 2 business days of learning of the loss, so the legal cap is $50.

questions.section_skill: Explain overdrafts and compute the cost of overdraft and related fees
questions.intro: An overdraft happens when a payment or purchase is larger than the money in the account and the bank pays it anyway. The account goes negative, and the bank may charge an overdraft fee. If the bank refuses the payment instead, the item is returned unpaid, and a returned-item ("NSF") fee may apply.
questions.question: What is an overdraft?

choices.text: Spending more than the account holds
Taking out a loan with a fixed monthly payment
Keeping a balance above the minimum required
Transferring money from checking to savings

questions.correct_answer: Spending more than the account holds

misconceptions.B: Confuses an overdraft with an installment loan
misconceptions.D: Confuses an overdraft with a transfer

questions.feedback: An overdraft means the account was overdrawn: the balance went below zero.

questions.section_skill: Explain overdrafts and compute the cost of overdraft and related fees
questions.intro: Each item paid while the account is overdrawn can trigger its own fee. Track the balance item by item. A small purchase can cost far more than its price once a fee is added.
questions.question: Mason's balance is $30. His bank charges $35 per overdraft. He makes three debit card purchases: $12, then $25, then $8, and he has opted in to overdraft coverage. If each purchase that makes the balance negative (or more negative) gets a fee, how much will he pay in fees?

misconceptions.D: Charges a fee on every purchase
misconceptions.A: Uses the amount overdrawn as the fee

questions.section_skill: Explain overdrafts and compute the cost of overdraft and related fees
questions.intro: Federal rules say a bank must get your permission (your "opt-in") before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases. If you do not opt in, those transactions are usually declined. Checks and automatic bill payments are treated differently and can still be overdrawn.
questions.question: Without opting in to overdraft coverage, what usually happens when Leah tries a one-time debit card purchase larger than her balance?

choices.text: The purchase is declined, with no overdraft fee
The purchase is approved, and she pays a $35 fee
The store gives her the item for free
Her account is closed immediately

questions.correct_answer: The purchase is declined, with no overdraft fee

misconceptions.C: Thinks the store absorbs the shortfall

questions.feedback: Without opt-in, one-time debit purchases above the balance are usually declined, so no overdraft fee applies.

questions.section_skill: Explain overdrafts and compute the cost of overdraft and related fees
questions.intro: Overdraft protection links checking to another account, such as savings or a line of credit. When checking runs short, money is moved automatically to cover the item. Banks often charge a transfer fee, but it is usually smaller than an overdraft fee.
questions.question: Hana links her savings account to checking for overdraft protection. The bank charges $10 per automatic transfer instead of a $35 overdraft fee. She overdraws twice this month. How much does linking save her this month?

misconceptions.A: Gives the transfer fees instead of the savings

questions.feedback: Without linking: 2 × $35 = $70. With linking: 2 × $10 = $20. Savings: $70 − $20 = $50.

questions.section_skill: Explain overdrafts and compute the cost of overdraft and related fees
questions.question: Ray's $80 electric bill payment is returned unpaid because his account is short. Which result is MOST likely?

choices.text: The bill is paid, and no one charges any fee
The electric company cancels the bill
He may owe a returned-item fee, and the bill is still unpaid
His bank pays the bill from its own funds and never charges him for it

questions.correct_answer: He may owe a returned-item fee, and the bill is still unpaid

misconceptions.A: Thinks a returned payment still counts
misconceptions.B: Thinks a failed payment erases the debt
misconceptions.D: Thinks the bank pays at no cost

questions.feedback: A returned (NSF) payment can cost a bank fee and a late fee from the biller, and the bill remains due.

questions.intro: When spending is larger than the balance and the bank pays anyway, the balance becomes negative. A negative balance means you owe the bank that amount.
questions.question: Rina's balance is $20. She spends $26. If the bank pays it, what is her balance (before any fee)?

misconceptions.B: Thinks the bank stops at zero

questions.intro: A negative account balance is a debt to the bank. You must deposit enough to bring the balance back to zero or above.

choices.text: The bank owes Rina $6

The buffer saves $100 and costs $408

The line of credit, by $32
They cost the same
The line of credit, by $27

questions.section_skill: Choose a savings account and explain how deposit insurance protects deposits
questions.intro: A savings account is a deposit account for money you are setting aside. It usually pays more interest than checking, and keeping savings separate makes it less likely you will spend it by accident. You can generally withdraw when you need to, though some banks limit how often.
questions.question: Why do people usually keep money for a goal six months away in a savings account rather than in checking?

choices.text: Savings accounts cannot be withdrawn from until the goal date
Savings usually earns more and stays apart from spending money
Checking accounts are not insured by the FDIC
Savings accounts guarantee the money will double

questions.correct_answer: Savings usually earns more and stays apart from spending money

misconceptions.A: Confuses savings with a certificate of deposit
misconceptions.D: Confuses saving with a guaranteed high return

questions.feedback: Savings earns more and keeps goal money apart from spending money. Both checking and savings are deposits that can be insured.

questions.section_skill: Choose a savings account and explain how deposit insurance protects deposits
questions.intro: Interest for one year ≈ balance × annual rate (as a decimal). To write a percent as a decimal, divide by 100: 3.5% = 0.035.

misconceptions.D: Gives the new balance instead of the interest

questions.section_skill: Choose a savings account and explain how deposit insurance protects deposits
questions.intro: The FDIC insures deposits at insured banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category (such as individual or joint). Credit union deposits have the same coverage through the NCUA. No depositor has lost insured funds since the FDIC began in 1934.
questions.question: Grace has $300,000 in one individual savings account at a single FDIC-insured bank. If the bank failed, how much of her deposit would be above the standard insurance limit?

misconceptions.A: Thinks every dollar is always insured
misconceptions.C: Confuses the insured part with the uninsured part

questions.feedback: $300,000 − $250,000 = $50,000 is above the standard limit for one owner at one bank in one category.

questions.section_skill: Choose a savings account and explain how deposit insurance protects deposits
questions.intro: FDIC insurance covers deposits: checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, and certificates of deposit. It does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds, crypto assets, annuities, or life insurance, even if a bank sells them. It also does not protect against investment losses.
questions.question: Leo buys shares of a stock mutual fund through an investment desk inside his bank's branch. The fund loses value. Does FDIC insurance cover the loss?

choices.text: Yes: anything bought at an FDIC-insured bank is insured
Yes, up to $250,000 of investment losses
No: investments are not deposits, even when sold at a bank
Only if Leo paid for the fund with money from his checking account

questions.correct_answer: No: investments are not deposits, even when sold at a bank

misconceptions.B: Applies the deposit limit to market losses
misconceptions.D: Thinks the source of money changes coverage

questions.feedback: Mutual funds are investments, not deposits, so FDIC insurance does not cover their losses.

questions.section_skill: Choose a savings account and explain how deposit insurance protects deposits
questions.question: Ava needs money she can reach quickly for unexpected costs and does not want it to lose value. Which place fits best?

choices.text: A stock fund that has risen sharply this year
A 5-year certificate of deposit with a penalty for early withdrawal
Cash hidden in her bedroom
An insured savings account

misconceptions.A: Chooses past performance over safety and access
misconceptions.C: Ignores theft, loss, and lost interest

questions.feedback: An insured savings account keeps money safe, available, and earning some interest.

choices.text: Money set aside for a laptop you plan to buy next spring
Money for this week's groceries
Money to pay this month's phone bill when it arrives next week
Cash for lunch tomorrow

questions.correct_answer: Money set aside for a laptop you plan to buy next spring
questions.feedback: Money for a later goal belongs in savings.

The bank adds money to her account

questions.intro: The interest rate is the yearly rate before compounding. APY (annual percentage yield) shows what you actually earn in a year once interest is added to your balance and itself earns interest (compounding). Banks must show APY for savings, so use APY to compare accounts.
questions.question:
Two savings accounts show:
Bank A: interest rate 4.00%, compounded monthly; APY 4.07%
Bank B: APY 4.05%

The interest rate of each, ignoring APY
The APY of each account
Whichever number is printed larger in the ad

questions.correct_answer: The APY of each account
questions.feedback: APY includes compounding, so comparing APY to APY is fair. Bank A (4.07%) earns slightly more than Bank B (4.05%).

questions.intro: APY is the actual percent your money grows in one year, so one year of earnings ≈ balance × APY.
questions.question: An account has an APY of 4.07%. About how much will $2,000 earn in one year if the rate stays the same and nothing is withdrawn?

misconceptions.D: Gives the balance, not the interest

APY includes extra deposits you plan to make later in the year
APY is the rate before taxes are added
Interest that is added during the year also earns interest

questions.correct_answer: Interest that is added during the year also earns interest
questions.feedback: With compounding, earlier interest earns interest too, so the yearly yield is above the stated rate.

questions.question: A savings rate is "variable." What does that mean?

choices.text: The bank can change the rate over time
The rate is fixed until the account is closed
The rate depends on how many times you log in
The rate is negative in some months

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories

misconceptions.C: Applies one limit across different banks
misconceptions.A: Thinks large balances are never insured

questions.feedback: Each bank insures his $200,000 individually: $400,000 total.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: Joint accounts are a separate ownership category from individual accounts. Each co-owner's share of joint accounts at one bank is insured up to $250,000.
questions.question: Sam and Pat own a joint account with $500,000 at one insured bank. Joint accounts are insured up to $250,000 per co-owner. How much is insured?

misconceptions.B: Applies one limit to the whole joint account

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: A check is a written order telling your bank to pay someone from your account. You write the date, the payee (who gets paid), the amount in numbers, the amount in words with cents as a fraction of 100, and your signature. The words are the legal amount if the two differ.

choices.text: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars
One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 7/10 dollars
Twelve hundred fifty-four point zero seven
One thousand two hundred forty-five and 07/100 dollars

misconceptions.C: Uses "point" instead of the cents fraction

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: To deposit or cash a check made out to you, you "endorse" it by signing the back. Adding "For deposit only" (a restrictive endorsement) means the check can only be deposited, which protects it if it is lost. For mobile deposit, banks often require "For mobile deposit only" too.
questions.question: Ben receives a paycheck made out to him and wants to deposit it at an ATM. What should he write on the back?

choices.text: Nothing; endorsing a check is optional
His PIN, so the ATM can verify him
His signature and "For deposit only"
His account balance, so the bank can update it

questions.correct_answer: His signature and "For deposit only"

misconceptions.B: Writes sensitive data on a check
misconceptions.D: Thinks the balance goes on the check

questions.feedback: Signing with "For deposit only" endorses the check and limits it to being deposited.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Peer-to-peer (P2P) payment apps move money quickly between people. Money you send yourself, even to a scammer, is usually treated as authorized and is often hard to get back. Federal error protections focus on transfers you did not authorize. Use P2P apps mainly with people you know and trust.
questions.question: Mia sends $60 through a payment app to someone selling concert tickets online. The tickets never arrive. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: The app must refund every payment that goes wrong
Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse
Her bank will reverse the payment automatically within one business day
The seller must legally deliver the tickets

questions.correct_answer: Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse

misconceptions.D: Thinks the law forces a scammer to deliver

questions.feedback: Because Mia authorized the payment, getting it back depends on the app's or bank's voluntary policies. Protections are stronger for unauthorized transfers.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Mobile check deposit lets you photograph a signed check in your bank's app. The bank may hold part of the money for a few days. Keep the paper check until the deposit is final, then destroy it securely so it cannot be deposited twice or misused.

choices.text: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it
Deposit the same check again at the bank to be safe
Throw it in the trash right after taking the photo
Give it back to the person who wrote it

questions.correct_answer: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it

misconceptions.C: Discards it before the deposit is confirmed

questions.feedback: Keep it until the funds are final in case the bank needs it, then shred it.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.question: Zara's landlord asks for rent in a way that leaves a record of payment. Which method fits BEST?

A credit card

An online bill payment or automatic transfer

misconceptions.C: Confuses prepaid value with an account payment

misconceptions.A: Confuses the price with what is left

choices.text: The account holder who signs and writes the check
The bank that prints the check

questions.question: Which situation makes a payment app MOST risky to use?

choices.text: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
Splitting a dinner bill with a close friend
Paying a family member back for groceries
Sending rent money to a roommate you have lived with for a year
