questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A wire transfer moves money between banks quickly, often the same day, and is generally final once sent. ACH transfers (used for direct deposit and online bill pay) move money between bank accounts more slowly and have some ways to return errors. Scammers often ask for wires because they are fast and hard to reverse.
questions.question: Which payment is generally the hardest to reverse once sent?

choices.text: A credit card purchase
A wire transfer
A check that has not been cashed yet
A debit card purchase you did not authorize

questions.correct_answer: A wire transfer

misconceptions.C: A stop payment may be possible

questions.feedback: Wires are fast and generally final, which is why scammers prefer them.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, so a real one is very reliable. But fake cashier's checks are common. The bank may make the money available before discovering the check is fake; when it bounces, you owe the bank the full amount.
questions.question: A buyer sends Liam a cashier's check for $1,500 for a $500 phone and asks him to wire back the extra $1,000. What is most likely happening?

choices.text: A generous buyer making an honest mistake
A normal practice for cashier's checks
A fake-check scam
A bank error that the bank will cover

questions.correct_answer: A fake-check scam

misconceptions.A: Ignores the classic overpayment scam pattern
misconceptions.D: Thinks the bank absorbs fraud losses

questions.feedback: Overpayment with a request to send money back is a classic fake-check scam. Liam would owe the bank when the check bounces.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.question: Which is a typical use of an ACH transfer?

choices.text: An employer's direct deposit of paychecks
Buying groceries with cash
Paying a bill with a paper money order bought at a store
Swiping a credit card at a store

questions.correct_answer: An employer's direct deposit of paychecks
questions.feedback: Direct deposit and many automatic bill payments use the ACH network.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: Criminals hack or fake emails and send new "updated" wire instructions so money goes to their account. Because wires are hard to reverse, verify instructions through a trusted phone number, not one in the suspicious email.
questions.question: Before wiring money for a home or apartment deposit, what is the safest step?

choices.text: Use the instructions in the most recent email, even if they changed
Wire the money quickly so you do not lose the apartment
Ask the sender to text you the account number again
Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

questions.correct_answer: Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

misconceptions.C: Uses the same possibly hacked channel

questions.feedback: Independent verification defeats changed-instructions scams.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.question: Ruth wrote a check and then learned it was lost in the mail before it was cashed. What service could stop it?

choices.text: A wire recall, which works on all checks
A stop payment order through her bank
Reporting the check to the IRS
Writing a second check for the same amount

questions.correct_answer: A stop payment order through her bank
questions.feedback: A stop payment order tells the bank not to pay that check, if it has not already cleared.

questions.intro: A common scam claims you received money "by mistake" and asks you to send it back. Sometimes the original payment was made with stolen information and is later reversed, leaving you with the loss. Verify inside your own app or bank, never through a link or message.
questions.question: Someone texts Ava: "I sent you $200 by mistake — please send it back!" Her app shows no new money in her account. What should she do?

choices.text: Send $200 back right away to be polite
Reply with her bank login so they can fix it
Check her own account directly and send nothing
Send $100 as a compromise

questions.correct_answer: Check her own account directly and send nothing

misconceptions.D: Still sends money to a scammer

questions.question: Which setting adds the most protection to a payment app?

choices.text: Sharing your login with a parent and a friend so they can watch for fraud
Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app
Using the same password as your email
Turning off notifications

questions.correct_answer: Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app
questions.feedback: Multi-factor authentication and an app passcode make unauthorized access much harder.

questions.intro: Real banks and payment apps do not ask you to move money to a "safe account" to protect it. Imposters pretend to be bank staff, tech support, or government officials and create urgency.
questions.question: A "customer support" caller says your payment app is hacked and asks you to send your balance to a "safe account." What is this?

choices.text: A standard security procedure
A government requirement
A way to earn extra interest
An imposter scam

questions.correct_answer: An imposter scam

misconceptions.A: Real companies do not ask this

questions.question: Which payment is generally protected under federal error rules (Regulation E)?

choices.text: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
A payment you chose to send to an online seller who never shipped
A payment you sent to the wrong person after typing their name
Money you lost gambling with an app

questions.correct_answer: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
questions.feedback: Regulation E protections focus on unauthorized transfers and certain errors; payments you authorize, even to scammers, are often not covered.

questions.question: Before sending money with a payment app to someone new, which step lowers the risk the MOST?

choices.text: Sending a small test payment to a stranger
Confirming who the recipient is through a source you trust
Checking that the stranger's profile has a photo and many friends
Asking the stranger to promise to deliver

questions.correct_answer: Confirming who the recipient is through a source you trust
questions.feedback: Verifying who you are paying, through a channel you trust, prevents most P2P losses.

questions.question: Jada earns $16.50 per hour and works 24 hours this week. What is her gross pay for the week?

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.intro: A sinking fund is for a KNOWN future cost with a known date. An emergency fund is for UNKNOWN surprises, such as a job loss or a sudden repair.
questions.question: Which is a sinking fund?

choices.text: Saving $50 a month for car insurance due every six months
Money spent on groceries each week of the month
An emergency fund for surprises you cannot predict
A loan used to pay a bill that is already past due

Irregular expenses are always paid by employers
Large, predictable bills arrive with no money set aside
Banks automatically pay irregular bills for free

A monthly phone bill
A daily bus fare
A car registration renewal

Spending each paycheck as soon as it arrives
Budgeting from your single best month
Avoiding any record of income

questions.feedback: A steady transfer smooths uneven income into predictable spending money.

questions.intro: A unit price is the price per unit, such as per ounce or per item: unit price = price ÷ quantity. Comparing unit prices shows which size is the better value. (A lower unit price helps only if you will use the larger amount before it spoils.)

The 12-ounce box: $0.30 per ounce
The 12-ounce box, because it costs less
The 20-ounce box: $0.30 per ounce

questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Every spending choice has an opportunity cost: the next-best thing you give up. Thinking about what else money could do helps you choose deliberately rather than automatically.

Nothing, because he still has the accessory
The progress toward the bike that he gives up
The sales tax on the accessory

questions.feedback: Choosing the accessory means giving up progress toward the bike, the next-best option.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices

Loss aversion about a past investment loss
The bandwagon effect from friends' choices
Anchoring on the "was" price

questions.feedback: The $200 anchor makes $120 seem cheap; comparing with $100 elsewhere shows it is not.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered. The sunk cost fallacy is letting it drive a new decision. Good decisions compare the future benefits and costs of each option.

The sunk cost fallacy
Anchoring
Comparison shopping

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Present bias is valuing what we want now much more than what we want later. Impulse buying feeds on it. Adding a delay, such as a 24-hour rule or removing saved cards, gives the planning part of the brain time to weigh in.
questions.question: Ana often buys things online late at night and regrets them. Which strategy targets this habit directly?

choices.text: Save her card details on every site so checkout is faster
Wait 24 hours before buying anything not planned
Turn on more shopping notifications
Shop only during sales events

questions.feedback: A waiting period interrupts impulse buying and lets her compare the purchase with her goals.

The reasons he wants a phone
